-53.92 L 69.69 -72.17"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" transform="matrix(0.91687 -0.39919 0.39919 0.91687 67.9 -71.4)"><path d="M 4.43 0 L 1.34 1.14 L 2.16 0 L 1.34 -1.14 Z"></path></g></g><g stroke-width="0.6pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M -74.09 -99.79 L -29.86 -119.88"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" transform="matrix(0.91049 -0.41354 0.41354 0.91049 -31.64 -119.07)"><path d="M 4.43 0 L 1.34 1.14 L 2.16 0 L 1.34 -1.14 Z"></path></g></g><g stroke-width="0.6pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 0 -101.68 L 0 -117.78"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" transform="matrix(0.0 -1.0 1.0 0.0 0 -115.83)"><path d="M 4.43 0 L 1.34 1.14 L 2.16 0 L 1.34 -1.14 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 5.03 -113.75)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:2.03em;--ltx-fo-height:0.47em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:6.81pt;" height="4.46" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 4.46)" width="19.07"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F1.pic1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">x402</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g><g stroke-width="0.6pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 74.24 -99.69 L 29.83 -119.88"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" transform="matrix(-0.9103 -0.41396 0.41396 -0.9103 31.61 -119.07)"><path d="M 4.43 0 L 1.34 1.14 L 2.16 0 L 1.34 -1.14 Z"></path></g></g><g stroke-dasharray="3.0pt,3.0pt" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-width="0.6pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 102.92 -99.69 L 102.92 -107.56 L 0 -107.56 L 0 -105.26"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" transform="matrix(0.0 1.0 -1.0 0.0 0 -107.21)"><path d="M 4.43 0 L 1.34 1.14 L 2.16 0 L 1.34 -1.14 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 36.4 -117.39)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:3.2em;--ltx-fo-height:0.51em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.14em;font-size:6.81pt;" height="6.15" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 4.8)" width="30.13"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F1.pic1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">publish</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Three-path execution model. The orchestrator routes requests to the local cache, shared graph (x402 payment), or browser fallback. Discovered routes are published back (dashed).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When an agent asks Unbrowse to perform an action on a website, the orchestrator routes the request automatically through a priority chain. First (<span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Path 1</span>), it checks the local route cache for a recent hit. If no cached route is available, it queries the shared graph (<span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Path 2</span>) for a matching skill; if found, the skill is installed locally and executed via direct API calls — no browser is launched, no DOM is parsed, and no LLM tokens are spent reasoning about page state. If a skill exists but fails, automatic fallback to browser capture and re-learning occurs transparently.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">If no suitable route exists in either cache or graph (<span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Path 3</span>), Unbrowse falls back to Kuri <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, a Zig-native CDP broker that replaces heavyweight browser automation frameworks. In our implementation measurements, Kuri’s packaged broker is substantially smaller and faster to start than a full Playwright runtime, though these figures should be understood as implementation-specific rather than independently benchmarked claims. Kuri launches headless Chrome, captures network traffic, reverse-engineers the API endpoints behind the UI, and publishes the learned skill to the shared graph for future reuse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">From the agent’s perspective, nothing changes: it describes what it wants in natural language, and Unbrowse handles routing transparently. Every time any agent discovers a new route, every other agent benefits. The graph is not mined through blind exploration but distilled from real demand — coverage naturally concentrates on the sites and workflows that agents actually need, analogous to cooperative caching in CDN systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. Crucially, agents can always bypass the shared graph and fall back to browser rediscovery; the graph wins only when it creates genuine value.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Unbrowse is distributed as an npm package that installs the CLI, bootstraps the Kuri browser runtime, and registers the tool with any detected agent host. It generates a <span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span> file following the AgentSkills.io open standard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> that any skill-compatible agent host can consume directly. Agents interact with Unbrowse through the CLI or its local HTTP API (<span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">POST /v1/intent/resolve</span>). All credentials remain in a local encrypted vault; published skills contain only endpoint documentation and schemas, never credentials.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">3.2. Capability Layer: Route Discovery Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As agents browse and complete tasks through Unbrowse, the system passively observes network traffic and infers reusable route abstractions, building on established techniques in network traffic analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and extending them into an agent-native pipeline. Discovered routes are published to a cloud-hosted marketplace backed by semantic vector search.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">3.2.1. Traffic Observation and Filtering</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Raw browser traffic contains significant noise from analytics, advertising networks, and CDN requests for static assets. We employ heuristic filtering based on Content-Type analysis (JSON/XML responses indicate API calls), URL pattern matching, request method analysis (POST/PUT/PATCH are strong API indicators), and response structure analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">3.2.2. Route Extraction and Normalisation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From filtered traffic, the system extracts endpoints and their parameter structures, response shapes, authentication assumptions, and route-specific metadata. These are converted into pointer-like route abstractions — not raw web content, but a maintained map of callable interfaces.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">3.2.3. What the Graph Stores</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The shared graph is primarily an index of pointers to callable interfaces, not a storage layer for the raw web. It stores route definitions and schemas, parameter structures and response shapes, and authentication descriptors. Derived attributes — confidence (computed from execution success rates), freshness (inverse decay from last verification date), and health (updated by the periodic verification loop described below in Skill Lifecycle and Schema Drift) — are recomputed continuously from execution telemetry rather than stored statically.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">3.2.4. Skill Packaging</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extracted routes are packaged into skills following the AgentSkills.io open standard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> — structured capability bundles that any compatible agent host can consume. Each skill contains:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SKILL.md</span> file providing human-readable endpoint documentation, compatible with any skill-aware agent host.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">auth.json</span> file holding captured authentication credentials that are encrypted and stored locally (never published to the marketplace).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">api.ts</span> file containing a generated TypeScript client for programmatic access.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Skills are the unit of sharing: what gets published to the marketplace is the knowledge of how to interact with a site, not credentials or execution capability. A single website may yield multiple skills (one per discovered workflow or endpoint group), and different agents may discover different endpoints on the same site. Skills are merged at the domain level when overlapping endpoints are detected, with attribution tracked per-endpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">3.3. Composite Scoring and Intent Resolution</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When an agent requests a task, the orchestrator follows a priority chain. First, it checks the <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">route cache</em> (24-hour TTL, persisted to disk) for an instant hit if the same intent was recently resolved. If no cache hit is found, the system performs a <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">marketplace search</em> using semantic vector search ranked by a composite score comprising 40% embedding similarity, 30% reliability, 15% freshness, and 15% verification status. These weights were set heuristically to prioritise semantic relevance while giving substantial weight to demonstrated reliability; they are configurable parameters, and adapting them from execution telemetry is planned future work. If no marketplace result is suitable, <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">live capture</em> launches a headless browser to record network traffic, reverse-engineer API endpoints, and publish a new skill. As a final fallback for static or server-side-rendered sites where no API endpoints are found, structured data is extracted from rendered HTML.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">3.4. Skill Lifecycle and Schema Drift</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Skills in the marketplace follow a natural lifecycle driven by real usage data. <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Active</em> skills are published, queryable, and executable. <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Deprecated</em> skills have triggered low-reliability warnings and remain discoverable but are ranked lower. <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Disabled</em> skills have confirmed endpoint failures and are removed from search results until re-verified. A background verification loop runs every 6 hours on each agent’s local Unbrowse server, executing safe GET endpoints to detect failures and schema drift. The type system includes a <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">consecutive_failures</span> counter for automatic deprecation; wiring this counter to a threshold-based deprecation policy is in progress.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Web APIs change without notice. The system continuously monitors for schema drift by comparing live response structures against documented response schemas. When critical drift is detected — removed fields, type changes — the affected endpoint is flagged for re-verification. This ensures the graph reflects current API reality rather than stale documentation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">4. Economic Model</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.1. The Adoption Condition</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The shared route graph replaces browser sessions with direct API calls for cached lookups. A cost-minimising agent will use the shared graph if and only if:</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{route}}&lt;c_{\text{rediscovery}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>route</mtext></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{route}}&lt;c_{\text{rediscovery}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{route}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>route</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{route}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the total fee an agent incurs through the shared graph (decomposed into Tier 1, 2, and 3 components in Section 5), and the expected rediscovery cost is decomposed as:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{rediscovery}}=c_{\text{latency}}+c_{\text{compute}}+c_{\text{tokens}}+p_{\text{fail}}\cdot c_{\text{retry}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>latency</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>compute</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>tokens</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>fail</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>retry</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{rediscovery}}=c_{\text{latency}}+c_{\text{compute}}+c_{\text{tokens}}+p_{\text{fail}}\cdot c_{\text{retry}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{latency}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>latency</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{latency}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the opportunity cost of multi-second page loads and sequential interaction overhead in browser-based agents, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{compute}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>compute</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{compute}}</annotation></semantics></math> is browser runtime cost (approximately 500 MB RAM per instance), <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{tokens}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>tokens</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{tokens}}</annotation></semantics></math> is LLM reasoning tokens for DOM interpretation and navigation, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{fail}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>fail</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{fail}}</annotation></semantics></math> is browser-task failure probability on realistic web benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{retry}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>retry</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{retry}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the cost of retrying a failed interaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This is a <em id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">necessary condition</em> for rational adoption, not a complete market model. It establishes the ceiling: no rational agent will pay <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{route}}\geq c_{\text{rediscovery}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>route</mtext></msub><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{route}}\geq c_{\text{rediscovery}}</annotation></semantics></math>, so the shared graph is disciplined by a real outside option. Section <a href="#S7" title="7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> provides empirical estimates for both sides of the inequality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.2. What Agents Pay For</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agents do not pay for access to the web itself. They pay for <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">speed</em>. Sub-second execution transforms what agents can do: multi-site research workflows that take minutes through browser automation complete in seconds through the marketplace. This speed advantage is categorical, not incremental — it determines whether agents can chain web interactions into real-time workflows or whether every web task becomes a blocking bottleneck.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Secondarily, agents also pay for lower compute burn (no browser runtime), lower LLM token burn (no reasoning about page state), lower failure risk, and maintained route knowledge kept fresh by the network.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The adoption condition as stated omits the marketplace search cost. In practice, each graph query incurs a Tier 3 search fee (Section 5.3) covering the semantic vector lookup (typically 50–200 ms latency, $0.001–0.005 per query). For a single interaction the Tier 3 fee is negligible relative to the multi-second browser alternative; however, for agents that query the graph frequently, cumulative Tier 3 spend must be included in the adoption calculus. A more complete model would express the condition as <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{search}}+f_{\text{install}}+n\cdot f_{\text{exec}}&lt;c_{\text{rediscovery}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>search</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>install</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>exec</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{search}}+f_{\text{install}}+n\cdot f_{\text{exec}}&lt;c_{\text{rediscovery}}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of executions on Tier 2 sites.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">4.3. Why a Shared Commons Can Emerge</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following Ostrom’s framework for knowledge commons <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, a shared route registry makes economic sense when many actors repeatedly rediscover similar routes, when pooled usage improves route quality faster than isolated usage, when maintenance is ongoing and expensive, and when duplication of discovery work is wasteful. The three-path execution model provides what Ostrom calls the “exit option” — competitors can always rebuild privately, and this credible threat disciplines the commons. The shared index wins only when it is cheaper than repeated rediscovery and when pooled usage improves coverage faster than isolated efforts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasise that this is a <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">conceptual</em> economic framework. Formal equilibrium analysis — including conditions under which the commons is underprovided, pricing strategies beyond the ceiling constraint, and welfare characterisation — remains future work. The current contribution is the architectural design that makes such a commons technically feasible, together with the empirical validation that the adoption condition (Equation <a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.1. The Adoption Condition ‣ 4. Economic Model ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) holds in practice.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">5. Route-Level Payment Architecture</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The economic model above establishes <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> agents should use the shared graph. This section describes <em id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> payments flow when they do. We distinguish three tiers:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tier 1 — Skill installation</span> (one-time): the agent pays once to download discovery documentation (endpoint schemas, auth patterns, client code). After installation the agent executes locally with no further marketplace payments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tier 2 — Site-owner execution fees</span> (opt-in): site owners who register with the marketplace attach a per-execution micropayment to routes that hit their endpoints. Only applies to opted-in sites.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tier 3 — Search / routing fees</span> (per-query): the agent pays a small fee each time it queries the shared graph for intent resolution or semantic route lookup, regardless of whether a skill is ultimately installed. This covers the cost of maintaining the index and serving vector search.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Tiers are additive. A typical interaction with a new Tier 2 site incurs all three; a repeat call to an already-installed non-opt-in route incurs none (the agent executes from its local cache). The remainder of this section details each tier.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.1. Tier 1: Skill Installation Payment</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Skill installation transactions follow the x402 protocol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, a recently proposed standard (2025) with early but growing production deployment. When an agent pays to install a route, it receives a skill — a structured capability package containing endpoint documentation, parameter schemas, auth profiles, and executable client code. This is a <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">one-time</em> payment for the discovery knowledge. After installation, the agent executes the skill locally using its own credentials with no further marketplace payments; the marketplace never executes on behalf of the agent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The payment handshake proceeds as follows: the agent requests skill installation from the shared graph; the server returns HTTP 402 with payment terms specifying amount, currency, network, and resource path; the agent signs the payment transaction and retries the request with payment proof; and the server verifies payment and returns the skill package for local installation. This enables true micropayments — as low as $0.005 per skill install — without intermediaries. The implementation uses a multichain wallet abstraction with pluggable provider adapters, settling in USDC on Solana by default, though the protocol is network- and provider-agnostic. The empirical evaluation in Section <a href="#S7" title="7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> measures route lookup performance independent of payment overhead; the 402 handshake adds negligible latency (a single additional round trip) to the skill installation step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.2. The Route Economy</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every route in the shared graph is a revenue-generating asset. When an agent pays the Tier 1 skill installation fee, that fee is automatically split via x402 among all parties who contributed to the route’s existence and maintenance.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">5.2.1. Fee Split Architecture (Tier 1)</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each skill installation fee <math id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is divided among route contributors <math id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, route maintainers <math id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, infrastructure <math id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> (approximately 10% platform toll), and an optional treasury/reserve <math id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S5.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=C+M+I+T" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=C+M+I+T</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In the initial design, contributors collectively receive approximately 70% of install revenue. This high contributor share is intentional: the system must make route discovery and maintenance economically attractive relative to the effort required. The specific split ratios are governance parameters, not derived from first principles; their optimality is an open question for future empirical study. Tier 2 per-execution fees flow directly to the site owner and are not subject to the contributor split.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">5.2.2. Delta-Based Contribution Attribution</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Routes are rarely discovered in a single act. More commonly, multiple contributors improve a route over time: one agent discovers the initial endpoint, another maps additional parameters, a third documents the auth flow, and a fourth adds error handling for edge cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Attribution is therefore <em id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">delta-based</em>. When a contributor commits an improvement to an existing route, the system records the marginal contribution — the delta between the route state before and after the commit. Delta magnitude is quantified using line-level schema changes and cosine dissimilarity between pre- and post-commit route embeddings (the specific embedding model is a replaceable implementation detail). The contributor share <math id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is distributed among all historical contributors in proportion to their cumulative delta scores.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We note that this attribution mechanism has not been formally analysed for incentive compatibility or Sybil resistance at scale. A contributor could in principle inflate their delta score through many small redundant commits. The current mitigation is a minimum-delta threshold below which commits are not attributed; formal analysis of manipulation resistance is deferred to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.3. Tier 2: Opt-In Per-Execution Payments</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tier 1 covers skill installation — the one-time payment for discovery documentation. Tier 2 is an independent, <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">opt-in</em> extension: site owners who register their domain with the marketplace can attach a per-execution fee to routes that hit their endpoints. When an agent executes a Tier 2 route, each API call triggers an x402 micropayment to the site owner in addition to the original skill installation fee. Sites that do not opt in are unaffected; agents pay only the Tier 1 skill install cost and execute freely thereafter.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The three-tier separation reflects three distinct value contributions: Tier 3 compensates the platform that <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">maintains the index</em>; Tier 1 compensates the contributors who <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">discovered</em> the route; Tier 2 compensates the site that <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">serves</em> the endpoint. The three revenue streams are independent and additive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The opt-in model transforms the relationship between agents and websites from potential adversarial extraction into consensual participation. This design draws on the emerging legal consensus following <em id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn</em> (2022) and subsequent rulings on automated web access <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>: opt-in participation with economic compensation provides substantially stronger legal standing than unilateral scraping. Sites that opt in gain a new monetisation channel for programmatic traffic, which is typically cheaper to serve than rendered pages.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">5.3.1. Websites as Usage-Priced Endpoints</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The opt-in model positions websites as usage-priced endpoints, aligning with the broader shift from subscription-based to consumption-based pricing (Stripe per transaction, OpenAI per token, Vercel per invocation). This shift is particularly relevant for agent traffic, which is bursty, unpredictable, and bypasses traditional session-based monetisation. Crucially, per-execution pricing applies only to Tier 2 opt-in sites. For all other routes, the agent pays once at skill install (Tier 1) and executes locally with its own credentials thereafter — the marketplace distributes knowledge (endpoint schemas, auth patterns), not ongoing access.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.4. Tier 3: Search and Routing Fees</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every query to the shared graph — whether via <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">POST /v1/intent/resolve</span> or the semantic skill search API — incurs a small per-query fee. This fee is independent of whether the query results in a skill installation; an agent that searches, inspects the results, and decides not to install still pays the search fee. The fee covers the operational cost of maintaining the shared index (vector embeddings, semantic ranking, infrastructure) and is typically an order of magnitude smaller than Tier 1 install fees (e.g. $0.001–0.005 per query).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tier 3 is the only tier that applies on every graph interaction. For agents that query frequently but install rarely, Tier 3 represents the primary cost of using the shared graph. The adoption condition (Equation <a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.1. The Adoption Condition ‣ 4. Economic Model ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) must therefore account for cumulative Tier 3 spend: if repeated search fees approach <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{rediscovery}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{rediscovery}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent should switch to Path 3 (browser fallback) and discover routes independently.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">5.5. Dynamic Route Pricing</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tier 1 skill installation fees are priced dynamically based on estimated rediscovery cost saved, route confidence and freshness score, current demand, and historical success rate. Tier 3 search fees are set by the platform and reflect index maintenance costs. The effective cumulative cost (Tier 3 search + Tier 1 install + any Tier 2 per-execution fees) is always bounded above by <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{\text{rediscovery}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mtext>rediscovery</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\text{rediscovery}}</annotation></semantics></math> from Equation <a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4.1. The Adoption Condition ‣ 4. Economic Model ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> — if the total cost of using the shared graph exceeds self-discovery, rational agents will defect to Path 3.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">6. Quality Proofing and Validation</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The trust and quality mechanisms described here determine which routes surface in the shared graph and, consequently, which routes appear in the benchmark evaluation (Section <a href="#S7" title="7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">6.1. Pre-Publish Validation</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before a route can be published to the shared graph, it undergoes automated validation. The validator checks the skill manifest for structural correctness (required fields, valid endpoint schemas, non-empty descriptions). Skills that fail hard validation checks are rejected; those with soft warnings are published with caveats. The design targets a minimum 50% endpoint success rate with at least one verified endpoint, though the current implementation validates manifest structure rather than executing live endpoint tests at publish time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">6.2. Execution and Verification Architecture</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All route execution is local. Agents execute routes using their own credentials on their own infrastructure — there is no cloud execution mode. Route verification — validating that a route is functional, that its response shapes match documented schemas, and that its health score is accurate — also runs locally via the same Kuri-backed browser runtime. Should a third-party validator network emerge in future, sandboxed verification environments could provide additional assurance, but the current local-execution model already ensures agents retain full control over outbound requests.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">6.3. Continuous Trust Model</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than rigid quality grades, route trust follows a continuous model inspired by ERC-8004 proportional trust <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. The current implementation composes three signals into a composite score.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first signal is <span id="S6.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">execution feedback</span>. The system tracks per-endpoint reliability scores based on execution outcomes (success, failure, timeout). These scores are updated after each execution attempt and feed into the composite ranking described in Composite Scoring and Intent Resolution. The design envisions cryptographically signed feedback to prevent Sybil manipulation, but this is not yet implemented; the current system relies on local execution telemetry.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The second signal is <span id="S6.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">automated verification</span>. A background verification loop runs every 6 hours, testing safe (GET) endpoints against live servers and checking for schema drift. Endpoints whose responses have diverged from their documented schemas are flagged for re-verification. The design envisions independent validators who stake to back their attestations (with false attestations slashable), but this validator marketplace is future work; current verification is fully automated and local.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The third signal is <span id="S6.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">freshness decay</span>. Trust decays over time using an inverse function: <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{freshness}=1/(1+d/30)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>freshness</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{freshness}=1/(1+d/30)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S6.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is days since last update. A route last verified 30 days ago is scored lower than one verified today, even if both had identical success rates at the time of verification. Endpoints stale beyond 24 hours are prioritised for re-verification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The combined trust score determines route visibility in the marketplace. Low-trust routes are ranked lower, while high-trust routes surface first. Routes whose endpoints are confirmed non-functional are marked as disabled and removed from search results.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">7. Implementation and Evaluation</h2>

<section id="S7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.1. System Implementation</h3>

<div id="S7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implemented the framework as an open-source system.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            Available at <a href="https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse</a>.</span></span></span> The runtime is built around Kuri <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, a Zig-native CDP broker that manages headless Chrome through an HTTP API. In our implementation, Kuri provides a lighter-weight browser control layer than a full Playwright stack, though exact binary-size and startup-latency figures are implementation measurements rather than independent benchmark results. All browser operations — navigation, HAR recording, cookie management, JavaScript evaluation, network interception — flow through Kuri’s HTTP endpoints, eliminating Node.js CDP bindings entirely.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Supporting components include a capture pipeline for network traffic analysis and API reverse-engineering, an extraction layer for endpoint schemas and auth profiles, a local encrypted credential vault, a marketplace server interface for skill publishing and semantic search, a verification system for periodic endpoint re-testing, and an execution engine with automatic auth refresh and retry logic.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.2. Benchmark Design</h3>

<div id="S7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All benchmarks were conducted on a single machine: Apple MacBook Pro with M4 Max chip, 64 GB unified memory, running macOS from Singapore over residential broadband (Singtel, approximately 28 Mbps downlink). TCP connect latency to target websites ranged from 24 ms (Wikipedia) to 88 ms (Amazon) depending on server location. This should be interpreted as a single-host live-web benchmark rather than a fully controlled systems evaluation: both Unbrowse and Playwright were measured under the same hardware and network conditions, but uncontrolled OS- and ISP-level variance may still affect absolute timings. A more controlled follow-up evaluation on fresh cloud VMs across multiple regions remains future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated performance across 94 domains drawn from the current graph, spanning government sites, SaaS platforms, developer tools, e-commerce, healthcare, finance, media, and social networks. Tasks were modelled after the WebArena benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> information-retrieval category. At time of writing, the graph contains routes for over 500 domains with approximately 10,000 endpoints, grown entirely through passive usage. Full benchmark results and raw data are available at <a href="https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse-bench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse-bench</a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">7.2.1. Task Design and Output Equivalence</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each benchmark task was an information-retrieval query returning a structured answer (e.g., “What is the current price of Product X on Site Y?” or “What are the top 5 trending items on Site Z?”). To ensure fair comparison, both paths were required to produce <em id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semantically equivalent</em> output:</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S7.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S7.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Playwright baseline:</span> Headless Chromium with full page load, JavaScript rendering, and targeted text extraction via CSS selectors that isolate the specific data fields matching the query. This is <em id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> raw DOM dump — it is structured extraction of the same fields the cached route returns.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unbrowse:</span> A single call to <span id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">POST /v1/intent/resolve</span>, measured on the third pass after two warmup rounds. The <span id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">timing.source</span> field verified each measurement was served from cache.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Output equivalence was verified by comparing the extracted data fields (not raw response size) between both paths. Tasks where the Playwright extraction could not produce the same structured output as the cached route were excluded from the benchmark. Both paths were run three times; the third pass was measured for both to control for DNS and TCP connection reuse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S7.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 7.2.1. Task Design and Output Equivalence ‣ 7.2. Benchmark Design ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows representative task examples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S7.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Representative benchmark tasks with output format.</span></figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.3. Warmed-Cache Performance</h3>

<figure id="S7.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S7.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Warmed-cache performance across 94 domains. Both paths run three times; third pass measured.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S7.T3.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

</figure>
<div id="S7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 7.3. Warmed-Cache Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports results for all 94 domains. Mean cached latency was <span id="S7.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">950 ms</span> versus <span id="S7.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3,404 ms</span> for Playwright — a <span id="S7.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.6<math id="S7.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> ratio of mean latencies. The median per-domain speedup is <span id="S7.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5.4<math id="S7.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span>, higher than the ratio of means because the speedup distribution is right-skewed (Figure <a href="#S7.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 7.3. Warmed-Cache Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Eighteen domains completed in under 100 ms, with the fastest at 79 ms versus 2,289 ms (30<math id="S7.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>). Both paths make requests to the same target servers over the same network; the 2,454 ms difference is browser execution overhead that cached skill execution eliminates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 7.3. Warmed-Cache Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the distribution of speedup ratios. The distribution is right-skewed: the majority of domains cluster between 3–9<math id="S7.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup, with a long tail extending to 30<math id="S7.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> for domains where API endpoints are particularly fast relative to their rendered pages (e.g., sites with heavy JavaScript that adds 2–4 seconds of render time but whose API returns JSON in under 100 ms).</p>
</div>

<section id="S7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.4. Cold-Start Performance</h3>

<div id="S7.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The warmed-cache results above represent the best case. When no cached skill exists (Path 3), the agent pays the full discovery cost: browser launch, page rendering, traffic capture, route extraction, skill publishing, and initial execution. To characterise this cost, we measured cold-start latency on a random sample of 20 domains not previously in the graph.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S7.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cold-start latency (Path 3: browser discovery + skill publish) across 20 previously unseen domains.</span></figcaption>

<tr id="S7.T4.5.1" class="ltx_tr">

<th id="S7.T4.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S7.T4.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">Latency</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<td id="S7.T4.5.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S7.T4.5.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">640 ms (median)</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S7.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Cold-start latency (Table <a href="#S7.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 7.4. Cold-Start Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) is substantially higher than both cached execution and Playwright baseline, reflecting the overhead of traffic capture and route extraction. However, this cost is paid <em id="S7.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">once</em> per route: the median subsequent cached call drops to 640 ms. The amortisation breakeven — the number of cached lookups needed to offset the cold-start premium over Playwright — is typically 3–5 uses for high-demand routes. Two domains failed skill extraction due to heavy client-side rendering with no identifiable API endpoints; these fell back to HTML extraction. We note that the cold-start sample (<math id="S7.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=20</annotation></semantics></math>) is small; larger-scale cold-start characterisation is ongoing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.5. Cost Analysis</h3>

<div id="S7.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#footnote4" title="footnote 4 ‣ Table 5 ‣ 7.5. Cost Analysis ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> compares estimated per-task costs across execution paths.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S7.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Estimated per-task cost comparison.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:111%;">4</span></span>
                
                
                
              LLM token costs assumed: $15/1M input, $75/1M output (Claude Opus 4, March 2026). These figures are illustrative; actual costs vary by provider and change frequently. Tier 1 install fees and Tier 3 search fees are based on dynamic pricing at time of writing. Tier 2 per-execution fees are set by site owners and shown as illustrative ranges.</span></span></span></span></figcaption>
<div id="S7.T5.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:166.4pt;vertical-align:-81.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(34.0pt,-16.4pt) scale(1.24525365840682,1.24525365840682) ;">
<table id="S7.T5.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S7.T5.5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S7.T5.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"></th>
<td id="S7.T5.5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S7.T5.5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Browser</span></td>
<td id="S7.T5.5.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S7.T5.5.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Tier 1</span></td>
<td id="S7.T5.5.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S7.T5.5.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Tier 2</span></td>
<td id="S7.T5.5.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S7.T5.5.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Tier 3</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S7.T5.5.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S7.T5.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S7.T5.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Component</span></th>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S7.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Under Tier 1 (the default), the skill install fee is amortised to zero after the first call, achieving 90–96% cost reduction per subsequent task. Tier 3 search fees apply only when querying the graph for new intents; once a skill is installed locally, subsequent executions bypass the graph entirely. Tier 2 adds a small per-execution fee for opt-in sites but remains well below browser rediscovery cost. All three tiers are additive and collectively bounded by the adoption condition (Equation <a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.1. The Adoption Condition ‣ 4. Economic Model ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">7.6. Network Growth</h3>

<div id="S7.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These per-interaction savings compound in long-running agentic workflows. An autonomous agent completing a multi-site research task may chain 20–50 web interactions. Cached API calls parallelise trivially where browser instances cannot: an agent querying 10 sites simultaneously completes in the latency of the slowest single call rather than sequentially through browsers, each consuming 500 MB+ of RAM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We observe early evidence of positive feedback dynamics: more agents generate more traffic, which discovers more routes, which attracts further agents. However, we have not yet measured the causal relationship between agent count and per-agent value rigorously enough to claim formal network effects. The 500-domain / 10,000-endpoint figure is a snapshot from the current graph; longitudinal analysis of growth trajectories and per-agent value as a function of graph size is ongoing work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">8. Discussion</h2>

<section id="S8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">8.1. Security Considerations</h3>

<div id="S8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Credential safety is maintained by keeping credentials local and encrypted; published routes contain only endpoint documentation and schemas. API stability is addressed through continuous validation and freshness scoring. Abuse prevention is achieved through rate limiting, reputation requirements, and economic costs that discourage abusive usage patterns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial routes.</span> A malicious contributor could publish a route that redirects requests to a phishing endpoint or exfiltrates query parameters. The current mitigation is multi-layered: pre-publish validation checks manifest structure and schema consistency; the continuous trust model tracks reliability scores from execution outcomes, so a malicious route’s trust score degrades after failures; and all execution is local, meaning agents can inspect outbound requests before sending credentials. However, a sophisticated attacker who publishes a route that passes initial validation but later serves malicious redirects remains a threat. Formal analysis of adversarial robustness, including route provenance attestation, cryptographically signed feedback, and anomaly detection on response destinations, is deferred to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">8.2. Ethical and Legal Considerations</h3>

<div id="S8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ability to programmatically access web services raises legitimate questions. Our approach differs from indiscriminate scraping in several ways: the economic layer provides natural rate limiting, routes are learned from normal browsing behaviour, and the system is designed for opt-in participation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As described in Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3. Tier 2: Opt-In Per-Execution Payments ‣ 5. Route-Level Payment Architecture ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>, our opt-in site owner compensation model transforms the relationship between agents and websites. The legal landscape for automated web access is evolving — the <em id="S8.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn</em> decision (2022) established that accessing publicly available data is not necessarily a violation of the CFAA, but subsequent rulings have introduced nuance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. Our opt-in model, with economic compensation for site owners, provides substantially stronger legal footing than unilateral scraping. We note that routes to sites that have not opted in occupy a grey area; the system does not circumvent authentication barriers. Support for <span id="S8.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">robots.txt</span> directive checking is planned but not yet implemented in the current codebase.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">8.3. Threats to Validity</h3>

<section id="S8.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">8.3.1. Benchmark Representativeness</h4>

<div id="S8.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 94-domain benchmark may be biased toward sites with permissive access policies. Of the 94 domains tested, 61 had no significant bot detection, 24 used basic rate limiting (respected by the system), and 9 employed Cloudflare or similar WAF protection. The speedup figures for heavily protected sites were lower (median 2.1<math id="S8.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> versus 6.8<math id="S8.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> for unprotected sites), as Unbrowse’s cached requests must still pass through bot-detection middleware. We did not test sites that actively block all non-browser traffic, as cached routes to such sites would fail entirely.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">8.3.2. Geographic Dependence</h4>

<div id="S8.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All benchmarks were run from Singapore. Absolute latency figures are geography-dependent; the <em id="S8.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">speedup ratios</em> (not absolute numbers) are the portable claim, as both Unbrowse and Playwright make requests to the same servers over the same network. From a US datacenter, absolute latencies would be lower for US-hosted sites, but the ratio of browser overhead to API call overhead would remain similar.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_font_italic ltx_title_subsubsection">8.3.3. Reliability Claims</h4>

<div id="S8.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The system tracks per-endpoint reliability scores and consecutive failure counts. However, the original claim that “skills with three or more consecutive failures are automatically deprecated” is partially implemented: the type system includes a <span id="S8.SS3.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">consecutive_failures</span> counter but the automatic deprecation threshold logic is not yet wired into the verification loop. Deprecation currently requires manual or backend-side intervention. Additionally, several open engineering issues affect runtime reliability on specific platforms, including Kuri crashes on Linux x64 (tracked in issue #50) and intermittent auth extraction failures across browsers (issue #88).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">8.4. Limitations</h3>

<div id="S8.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We note that the following limitations are not unique to Unbrowse but are shared by any agentic web interaction approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Current limitations include anti-bot measures (sophisticated bot detection blocking non-browser requests), dynamic authentication (OAuth flows requiring human interaction), and session persistence (periodic re-authentication as tokens expire). The speedup figures reported in Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 7.3. Warmed-Cache Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> represent warmed-cache performance in a single-host live-web setting; real-world gains vary with anti-bot middleware, token expiration, regional latency, and deployment environment. Cold-start performance (Table <a href="#S7.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 7.4. Cold-Start Performance ‣ 7. Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) demonstrates that the initial discovery cost is substantial, and the system’s value proposition depends on sufficient reuse to amortise this cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The economic model (Section <a href="#S4" title="4. Economic Model ‣ Internal APIs Are All You Need Shadow APIs, Shared Discovery, and the Case Against Browser-First Agent Architectures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) is a conceptual framework, not a formal equilibrium analysis. Deployment-scale data on contributor attribution incentive compatibility, Sybil resistance, and long-run pricing dynamics remain areas for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection">8.5. Future Directions</h3>

<div id="S8.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several directions for future research emerge:</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S8.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S8.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Formal economic analysis:</span> Equilibrium characterisation, optimal pricing strategies, welfare analysis, and incentive compatibility proofs for the delta-based attribution mechanism including Sybil resistance guarantees.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Route composition:</span> Automatic chaining of multiple routes for complex multi-site workflows, and federated route networks enabling private sharing within organisations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Deployment-scale validation:</span> Empirical measurement of x402 micropayment flows, site owner adoption of the opt-in compensation model, and longitudinal study of graph growth dynamics to validate the network effects hypothesis. A key open question is whether websites can reliably distinguish agent traffic from human browsing; if not, the opt-in pricing model must account for mixed traffic to avoid charging human users.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparative evaluation:</span> Formal comparison with existing API aggregation platforms (RapidAPI, Postman) on coverage, latency, and cost metrics.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#1461BD;">9. Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented Unbrowse, a shared route graph — a collectively maintained index of callable web interfaces. By combining passive route discovery from real browsing traffic with a three-tier micropayment model via x402 — per-query search fees (Tier 3), one-time skill installation (Tier 1), and opt-in per-execution site-owner compensation (Tier 2) — the system offers a way for agents to interact with the existing web through discovered machine-usable interfaces rather than only through rendered pages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In a single-host live-web benchmark of equivalent information-retrieval tasks across 94 domains, fully warmed cached execution averaged 950 ms versus 3,404 ms for Playwright (3.6<math id="S9.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> mean, 5.4<math id="S9.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> median), with well-cached routes completing in under 100 ms. Cold-start discovery averages 12.4 s but is paid once per route; the amortisation breakeven is typically 3–5 uses. These savings may compound in multi-step workflows, though broader deployment validation remains future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The system’s market discipline — grounded in a real outside option where agents can always defect to browser rediscovery — distinguishes it from purely speculative protocol designs. Formal economic analysis, incentive compatibility proofs, controlled multi-region benchmarking, and deployment-scale validation remain open problems; the present contribution is an architectural proposal with an implemented system and initial empirical evidence that shared route lookup can outperform redundant browser rediscovery on the evaluated tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>

<span class="ltx_bibblock"><em id="bib.bib32.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">arXiv:2508.13787</em>, 2025.

</span></li>
      
<li id="bib.bib33" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">[33]</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">
D. Perera.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">webMCP: Efficient AI-native client-side interaction for agent-ready web design.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><em id="bib.bib33.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">arXiv:2508.09171</em>, 2025.

</span></li>
    
</ul>
</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Reproducibility</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments were conducted on an Apple MacBook Pro (M4 Max, 64 GB unified memory) running macOS 15.3 from Singapore over residential broadband (Singtel, <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>28 Mbps downlink). Software versions: Kuri v0.1 (Zig 0.13), Node.js 22.x, Playwright 1.48, headless Chromium 131. The benchmark harness, raw latency data, and analysis scripts are available at <a href="https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse-bench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/unbrowse-ai/unbrowse-bench</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Benchmark Domain List</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 94 domains span the following categories: government (12), SaaS/developer tools (18), e-commerce (14), healthcare (8), finance (11), media/news (15), social networks (7), and other (9). The full list with per-domain latency measurements is provided in the benchmark repository. Representative examples include Wikipedia, GitHub, Hacker News, Amazon, Weather.gov, and various regional government portals. Domains were selected from the existing route graph without cherry-picking; the only exclusion criterion was that both Unbrowse and Playwright paths must produce semantically equivalent structured output for the same query.</p>
</div>
</section><div class="ltx_rdf" about="" property="dcterms:creator" content="Lewis Tham, Nicholas Mac Gregor Garcia, Jungpil Hahn"></div>
